title: I'm Spartacus!
summary: Josh and Chuck open with off-topic banter about Stanley Kubrick films, Eliza Skye-style sketch comedy, Survivor, Naked and Afraid, and Star Wars sequels. They then tell the story of Spartacus, a Thracian who was reportedly a Roman auxiliary soldier before being enslaved and trained as a murmillo gladiator at a school in Capua. He escaped with about seventy gladiators in 73 BC, armed himself from a captured supply caravan, and was joined by his Thracian wife (a prophetess of Dionysus) and by Crixus. They defeated praetor Claudius Glaber near Mount Vesuvius, then beat praetor Publius Varinius and consuls Gellius Publicola and Lentulus Clodianus, swelling to tens of thousands. After a split with Crixus, whose group was destroyed, Spartacus was defeated by Marcus Licinius Crassus, who decimated deserters and hunted survivors. Spartacus died in battle and his body was never found. The hosts discuss the 1960 Kubrick film written by Dalton Trumbo, the Howard Fast novel, and Spartacus's later legacy. The episode closes with a listener email from a retired wastewater analyst about the wastewater treatment episode, which the hosts acknowledge.

segments.title: Opening banter on Kubrick and TV
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Stanley Kubrick films, the sketch show Eliza Skinner is in, Survivor and Naked and Afraid, and past TV appearances. They also mention their sources for the Spartacus episode.

segments.title: Spartacus's early life and capture
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Spartacus as a Thracian, note the scarce ancient sources, and describe a text saying he was a Roman auxiliary soldier later drummed out of the army. He was captured, sold into slavery, and sent to a gladiator school in Capua run by a man called Vacca. They compare him to a defector stormtrooper in Star Wars.

segments.title: Life of a gladiator
segments.summary: The hosts explain that gladiators were low-status slaves, prisoners, or criminals, and that fights were not always to the death. They describe gladiator training and types, including the murmillo that Spartacus fought as, with a helmet, tall shield, and gladius, and the retiarius with a net and trident.

segments.title: Escape from the gladiator school
segments.summary: In 73 BC, about seventy gladiators led by Spartacus broke out, overpowered guards with kitchen cleavers, and seized gladiator weapons from a passing caravan. Plutarch's account of Spartacus's Thracian wife, a prophetess of Dionysus, is discussed, including the snake omen. The band trained near Mount Vesuvius.

segments.title: Defeating Glaber and growing the revolt
segments.summary: Praetor Claudius Glaber blockaded the only road up Vesuvius, but the rebels climbed down vine ropes, attacked the Roman camp, and killed the soldiers. Word spread, and tens of thousands of slaves and commoners joined, with Spartacus reportedly splitting the spoils equally. The hosts also note atrocities committed by his followers.

segments.title: Battles with Varinius, the consuls, and Crixus split
segments.summary: Praetor Publius Varinius was nearly captured and lost his horse. The rebels grew to about 120,000 by some estimates. Spartacus built a cavalry over winter and beat consuls Gellius Publicola and Lentulus Clodianus. After a dispute, Crixus split off with about 30,000 men and was killed by the Romans.

segments.title: Crassus, decimation, and Spartacus's death
segments.summary: Marcus Crassus, a very wealthy praetor, financed a campaign against the rebels, reassembled defeated armies, and decimated five hundred deserters. Spartacus was killed in battle while trying to reach Crassus. His body was never found. Survivors were crucified. Rome passed some reforms afterward.

segments.title: Spartacus legacy and film
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how abolitionists and Marxists later admired Spartacus, and how Dalton Trumbo wrote the script for the 1960 Kubrick film based on a Howard Fast novel that Fast wrote in jail. They note the movie's inaccuracies, such as the crucifixion scene.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: A retired wastewater analyst wrote in about the earlier wastewater treatment episode, saying treatment plants operate under Clean Water Act permits. The hosts agree and thank him, then sign off.
